column1: Understanding the food component of inflation

The thesis Understanding the Food Component of Inflation by Emanuel Kohlscheen  published as BIS Working Paper No. 1056  explores the dynamics of food price inflation across 35 countries over the past 30 years. The study confirms the applicability of the Phillips curve to food inflation  indicating that economic overheating systematically increases the food component of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It also highlights the influence of general inflation expectations from professional forecasters on food price inflation. The research quantifies how increased food production and imports  or reduced food exports  can mitigate food inflation. However  the connection between domestic and global food prices is generally weak  with pass-throughs within a year ranging from 0.07 to 0.16 after accounting for exchange rate variations. The study underscores that food price developments are not exogenous but are closely linked to broader economic conditions  suggesting that macroeconomic stabilization policies also impact domestic food prices.

The research further examines the effects of domestic food production and international trade on food inflation. A 10% increase in crop yields is found to reduce food CPI inflation by approximately 0.5%. The impact of a similar increase in food imports is smaller and not always statistically significant  indicating imperfect substitutability in mitigating local crop shortfalls. Conversely  a 10% increase in food exports has a smaller net effect of 0.3%  likely due to the concentration of exports on specific products not representative of typical consumer food baskets.

The study also finds that the link between domestic and global food prices is weak  with pass-throughs within a year ranging from 0.07 to 0.16 after considering exchange rate variations. This suggests that global food price indices are an imperfect proxy for domestic food price developments. Additionally  while energy costs significantly impact food costs statistically  their economic effect is negligible.

This research fills a gap in the literature by providing novel cross-country evidence on the factors driving the food component of CPIs. It contributes to a better understanding of retail food price pressures  which is crucial for formulating effective food policies and broader policies aimed at price stability. The study's findings are particularly relevant for policymakers  as they may influence the calibration of monetary policy  especially in countries where the inflation target is based on headline inflation. The research also highlights the importance of understanding the transmission of global food prices to domestic retail food costs and the role of domestic food production and trade in alleviating food price pressures.
